title: Don't seek the true
hookLine: the poem: don't seek the true, just stop holding opinions

cards: How many opinions have you held since you woke up? About the weather. The traffic.
Someone's haircut, a headline, the way the coffee came out. Nobody asked for most of them, and plenty are gone by lunch. They arrive on their own, like notifications.

Now here is a religious poem, chanted in some Chan and Zen halls, and in the middle of it comes a line that sounds almost backwards. You might expect it to say: seek the truth with all your heart. It says the opposite.

teach.h: THE LINE: DON'T SEEK THE TRUE.
teach.b: In paraphrase, the Xinxin Ming says: do not seek the true; just stop holding opinions. A startling thing to put in a poem about the way. Isn't truth the point?

Look at the word just. The poem isn't saying truth doesn't matter. It's saying that hunting for it, as if it were a prize somewhere else, is one more kind of grabbing, one more round of picking and choosing.
The poem has already called the way round and complete, like vast space, with nothing lacking. So the instruction isn't go and find it. It's stop doing the thing that covers it.
Then, holding versus having. Opinions will keep arriving; the line doesn't ask you to stop thinking. It asks you to stop clutching.

An opinion you can set down is a thought. One you can't set down has become a wall, and you end up seeing the wall instead of the person, the movie, the rainy afternoon. Yesterday's hair's breadth was the first lean.
An opinion is that lean after it has set hard. And what's left when you put one down? Not emptiness.

The coworker, before your verdict on her. The song, before you decided it was overplayed. The poem's wager is that this plain thing, without commentary, is closer to what you were seeking in the first place.

how: In Zen and Chan practice this line is sometimes quoted in talks and used during sitting as a reminder to let commentary about the sitting, and about everything else, go by without holding on to it.

games.q: what does “don't seek the true” mean?
o: truth doesn't matter, so stop caring about it
stop clutching views; what was sought is here
keep your opinions private to avoid arguments

games.q: don't seek the true: tap the pairs.
p: truth isn't a prize somewhere else
an opinion you can't set down
a wall in front of the thing

s: the poem says truth doesn't matter
it says not to hunt for truth as a prize elsewhere; stop holding opinions, and nothing is lacking.
the line asks you to stop clutching opinions, not to stop thinking
thoughts will keep arriving; the poem asks you not to grip them.
setting down your opinion means taking the other side's
putting down one view isn't picking up another; the poem asks you to stop picking sides.

games.q: a friend asks your take on a show you half-watched. today's line comes to mind. what fits it best?
o: say you don't have one, and ask what they saw
argue the opposite to keep things lively
games.why: the poem doesn't forbid speaking. it asks you to stop gripping views, and having no take leaves room for the show, and your friend, as they are.

practice: Within a few breaths, a comment will show up about the sitting itself: this is going well, I'm bad at this, my knee. Those are opinions too, so each time one comes, see it and set it down, the way you'd set a cup on a table.
You don't have to argue with it.

wordCard.voice: Don't seek the true. The Xinxin Ming's line that turns the search around: don't hunt for truth somewhere else, just stop holding opinions. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese (xi jian): 'stop views', the poem's 'just stop holding opinions'.

carryVoice: Your line: just stop holding opinions. Thoughts still come; they just don't have to be clutched. More of the poem tomorrow.
